title: Antigen-chosen pharmacological control of immune memory

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an administered pharmacological treatment that durably changes the immune response to a chosen antigen while preserving useful responses to unrelated antigens. Its tolerance component would teach the immune system to stop attacking a particular target associated with disease. The broader ambition also includes reversing that tolerance when needed or deliberately establishing a chosen protective response. These are distinct capabilities; demonstrating one would not establish the others.

A concrete starting point is KAN-101, an investigational product that combines a gliadin peptide with a liver-targeting glycosylation signature and is designed to induce immune tolerance to gliadin in coeliac disease. This illustrates how an administered product could present a selected antigen in a setting intended to promote tolerance. The supplied human study establishes an early clinical investigation of that approach, rather than achievement of durable immune-memory control.

Conceptual clarification: controlling an antigen-specific response does not necessarily mean deleting the cells that remember it. Durable tolerance, selective erasure of memory, and reversible suppression of a response could produce different biological states. Likewise, protective priming substantially overlaps with vaccination. The distinctive ambition here is precise, durable and potentially reversible pharmacological control, whose individual components would each need demonstration.

significance.text: Conditional significance: durable tolerance to a pathogenic antigen, with unrelated protective responses retained, could let clinicians treat the immune response responsible for disease while reducing dependence on broad immunosuppression in suitable patients. The direct advance would be antigen-level selectivity combined with lasting clinical benefit. That combination could change treatment from repeated suppression of disease activity to sustained control after a finite treatment course.

Conditional downstream possibilities include treatment of selected autoimmune diseases, allergies and transplant-related immune responses. These applications would require separate evidence: the relevant antigen or antigens must be identifiable and addressable, the pathogenic response must remain controlled, and protection against infection and cancer must be assessed. A result against one known antigen would not establish that the same approach can accommodate the antigenic complexity of every disease or replace existing treatment across these fields.

The analogy to editing immune memory is useful only as a description of the intended selectivity. It should not imply that tolerance physically erases memory, that an established response can be switched back on at will, or that every patient's immune history can be rewritten predictably. Adding protective responses would also need a clearly defined advantage over existing vaccination. None of these broader capabilities is established by the supplied KAN-101 tolerance study.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unresolved capability within this record is durable clinical control of a chosen pathogenic immune response in humans, achieved pharmacologically while preserving unrelated protection. Reversibility and protective priming extend that objective and require additional evidence. The supplied abstract does not establish these outcomes, but its limited scope also cannot establish that they are absent everywhere in pharmacology.

Engineering synthesis: the challenge extends beyond temporarily inhibiting an inflammatory signal. An antigen-directed treatment must reach the appropriate biological setting, expose the relevant antigen in a way that reliably promotes the intended response, and maintain that response after treatment ends. The earlier description of tolerance as a cellular program usefully emphasizes this persistence problem, but the supplied abstract does not independently establish that mechanistic account or identify which cellular processes limit success.

Further proposed barriers are selecting the disease-driving antigen or antigen set, choosing an effective dose and delivery schedule, avoiding unintended activation of the targeted response, and distinguishing lasting tolerance from a transient change in a biomarker. Selectivity also has to be demonstrated independently: improvement in the target disease does not by itself show that unrelated immunity remains intact.

For the broader ambition, reversibility would require a dependable way to restore an appropriate response after tolerance has been induced. Selective memory erasure would require evidence that distinguishes loss of memory from continued regulation of an existing response. Protective priming would require a defined capability beyond ordinary vaccine-induced immunity. These are separate scientific objectives rather than automatic consequences of successful antigen-specific tolerance.

current_state.text: The supplied human evidence is the completed first-in-human ACeD phase 1 study of KAN-101 in coeliac disease, reported by Murray and colleagues in 2023 and published in the August 2023 issue of The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. KAN-101 contains a gliadin peptide conjugated to a liver-targeting glycosylation signature and was designed to induce tolerance to gliadin. The primary endpoint was the incidence and severity of adverse events.

The authors reported an acceptable safety profile. The abstract described future evaluation of safety and efficacy, including biomarker responses during a gluten challenge, at doses of 0.6 mg/kg and greater. That dose statement concerns planned evaluation; it is not an established effective-dose threshold. The supplied abstract does not establish durable clinical remission, reversibility, selective memory erasure, protective priming or preserved unrelated protective immunity.

The abstract stated that coeliac disease had no approved therapies at the time of the report. This is a historical statement from the 2023 publication. The review inspected only the PubMed abstract and bibliographic record, not the full article or its detailed analyses. Although the saved record was retrieved on November 1, 2026, later publications, efficacy outcomes and trial-registry updates were not checked, and no freshness search was supplied. The dated study therefore cannot establish the field's status on that later date; the access limitation does not invalidate its reported early safety findings.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration for the tolerance component: controlled human trials in at least two unrelated immune diseases with known relevant antigens should show durable clinical remission after the pharmacological treatment course, off broad immunosuppression, together with retained responses to an unrelated vaccine or infectious antigen. The two-disease threshold is an author-selected test of breadth, not an established standard. Successful finite trials would demonstrate benefit within their studied diseases and populations, rather than universal antigen-level control.
completion_criteria.label: Selective durable remission off broad immunosuppression in two unrelated diseases

completion_criteria.text: Proposed trial requirements: prespecify the duration that counts as durable, permitted background treatment, clinically meaningful remission endpoints, disease-relevant exposure or challenge conditions, and measures of retained protective responses. Follow-up should establish whether benefit persists after dosing ends and document relapse, retreatment and adverse outcomes. Responses to a limited set of unrelated antigens would support selectivity within those tests; they would not prove preservation of all immunity against infection or cancer.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified durability criteria and follow-up document sustained benefit and harms

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: confirm the result in independent cohorts or trials, characterize which patients and antigen profiles respond, and establish a reproducible product, dose and administration schedule. A safety study or a short-lived biomarker change after antigen challenge would not by itself demonstrate durable clinical tolerance. An engineered cell therapy manufactured outside the body would also fall outside this record's chosen pharmacological scope, even if it produced a related immune effect.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication establishes responders and reproducible pharmacological treatment

completion_criteria.text: Separate proposed demonstrations are needed for the broader claims. Reversibility should require restoration of an appropriate antigen-specific response after induced tolerance, with acceptable safety and prespecified clinical or functional evidence. A claim of selective memory erasure would require evidence distinguishing erasure from ongoing regulation. Protective priming should demonstrate a clinically useful protective response and specify the additional control offered beyond existing vaccination. Passing the tolerance benchmark alone would not complete these other components.
completion_criteria.label: Distinct evidence establishes reversibility, selective memory erasure and protective priming

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison — PHA-03, General prevention of idiosyncratic immune-mediated drug injury: both concern avoiding harmful immune responses. PHA-04 focuses on controlling a selected antigen-specific response; PHA-03 concerns general prevention of immune injury caused by drugs. An antigen-directed tolerance approach might help with particular drug-associated responses if their relevant targets were known, but that would not establish general prevention of idiosyncratic injury.

Roster comparison — PHA-02, Prospective prediction of human efficacy, dose, and major toxicity before first-in-human exposure: better prediction could assist development of antigen-directed products, but prediction and therapeutic control are separate achievements. PHA-04 requires demonstrated clinical efficacy, durability and selectivity even if a predictive method successfully forecasts them.

Roster comparison — PHA-06, In-place pharmacological replacement of missing human cell types: both envision administered products producing lasting changes in biological function. PHA-04 seeks to redirect an immune response and does not require replacement of a missing cell type. Its exclusion of externally manufactured cell therapy is a scope choice, not evidence that it accomplishes cell replacement.

Roster comparison — PHA-05, Systemic pharmacological access to brain parenchyma for arbitrary drug classes, and PHA-11, Reliable oral systemic exposure for folded peptides and proteins: delivery can constrain antigen-directed treatment, but these entries address different delivery barriers. Liver-targeted delivery in the KAN-101 example does not establish general brain access or reliable oral exposure. Conversely, solving either delivery problem would not by itself establish antigen-specific tolerance.

Roster comparison — PHA-13, A medicine that holds its own therapeutic window without an external controller: a durable immune effect and autonomous control of drug exposure are distinct properties. PHA-04 would still require appropriate dosing and safety monitoring; lasting tolerance does not imply that a medicine regulates its own therapeutic window.

Roster comparison — PHA-08, Anti-infective drugs that eradicate dormant persisters without seeding genetic resistance: preserving protective immunity during antigen-directed treatment is relevant to infection risk, but it is different from eliminating persistent pathogens. Neither achievement would establish the other. These relationships leave the supplied roster entries distinct.

change_log.reason: One phase 1 abstract cannot establish a field-wide absence of selective immune-memory control.

change_log.reason: It helps explain the persistence challenge, but the supplied abstract does not substantiate a general mechanistic account.

change_log.change: Made the significance conditional and distinguished antigen-level selectivity from replacement of broad immunosuppression across whole disease categories.
change_log.reason: Clinical applicability depends on disease-specific antigens, durable benefit and retained protective immunity.

change_log.reason: These details clarify demonstrated scope without presenting a future efficacy evaluation as an achieved result.

change_log.reason: Retrieval in 2026 does not make a 2023 report a verified account of current treatment availability or later trial outcomes.

change_log.reason: Finite demonstrations establish studied breadth and selectivity, while adjacent pharmacological capabilities remain separate innovations.

unresolved_issues: Later KAN-101 efficacy results, registry updates and the field's status on November 1, 2026 remain unassessed.
The full trial article and detailed efficacy analyses were not inspected; conclusions are limited to the supplied abstract and bibliographic record.
The supplied evidence does not resolve whether KAN-101 produces durable remission or preserves unrelated protective immunity.
The cellular mechanisms necessary for durable, reversible control and the principal barriers across different diseases are not established by this source.
The novelty of protective priming beyond existing vaccination still requires a specific definition.
Durability periods, remission endpoints, acceptable background treatment and the breadth of protective-immunity testing remain to be specified for any actual completion trial.
No substantive review recommendation was rejected; mechanistic explanation was retained only as labeled synthesis rather than a source-established finding.

brief.title: Medicines that reshape immunity to a chosen target
possible: People whose immune systems attack a disease-related target could receive a finite course of medicine that stops that attack for the long term, while keeping useful responses to other targets.
The broader goal includes restoring a response after deliberately quieting it, or establishing a chosen protective response. Each capability would need its own demonstration.
why: For people with suitable autoimmune diseases, allergies or transplant-related immune reactions, lasting control could reduce dependence on medicines that broadly suppress immunity. Treatment could move from repeatedly suppressing disease activity to sustained benefit after dosing ends.

sources.showed: An early human trial found an acceptable safety profile for KAN-101, a medicine designed to quiet the response to a gluten component in coeliac disease. Treatment-related side effects were mild to moderate.
sources.quote: Rapid systemic clearance of KAN-101 was observed and no accumulation on repeated dosing.
sources.cited_for: This supports the feasibility of administering a medicine designed to quiet a chosen immune response.
sources.not_established: The trial did not establish lasting remission or preservation of unrelated protective responses.

sources.who: Stacie M Jones and colleagues for the Immune Tolerance Network
sources.showed: Giving peanut by mouth as treatment produced remission in some young children after treatment stopped. Younger children were more likely to reach remission. Dosing reactions were common.
sources.quote:
By use of multivariable regression analysis of participants receiving peanut oral immunotherapy, 
younger age and lower baseline peanut-specific IgE was predictive of remission.
sources.cited_for: This demonstrates that a chosen allergic response can remain quiet after treatment ends in some patients.
sources.not_established: Remission after a limited avoidance period does not establish permanent tolerance or preserved protection against unrelated targets.

sources.who: Ciarán P. Kelly, Joseph A. Murray and the TAK-101 Study Group
sources.showed: In a small, short trial, TAK-101 reduced gluten-triggered immune activation in people with coeliac disease. It packages a gluten component inside tiny particles.
sources.cited_for: This supports selectively reducing the immune response to a disease-related target in humans.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish lasting symptom control or broad preservation of protective immunity.

sources.showed: In adults with recently diagnosed diabetes caused by immune attack on insulin-producing cells, injections of a fragment of an insulin precursor were well tolerated. Daily insulin use remained unchanged in treated groups but rose with placebo.
sources.quote:
Treatment was well tolerated with  
no systemic or local hypersensitivity.
sources.cited_for: This provides early human evidence of treatment directed at a disease-related immune target beyond coeliac disease.
sources.not_established: The findings do not establish lasting remission after treatment or preservation of unrelated protective responses.

shown: The Immune Tolerance Network demonstrated peanut-allergy remission in some young children after treatment stopped, lasting through a 26-week avoidance period. This is evidence of benefit beyond dosing, though its longer duration remains unknown.

The TAK-101 Study Group reduced gluten-triggered immune activation in a small coeliac disease trial. Murray and colleagues established early safety findings for KAN-101. Neither result establishes lasting clinical remission with unrelated immunity preserved.
missing: Controlled human trials have yet to establish the combined goal of lasting disease remission after dosing and retained unrelated protective responses.
Independent studies must establish which patients respond and a reproducible medicine, dose and treatment schedule.
Restoring a quieted response, selectively erasing immune memory and adding protection beyond vaccination each need separate demonstrations.

milestones.label: Lasting selective remission across two unrelated diseases
milestones.explanation: Controlled trials would have to show lasting remission after treatment in two unrelated diseases with known targets, without broad immune suppression and with unrelated protection retained. This would establish breadth and selectivity.

milestones.label: Defined follow-up establishes lasting benefit and harms
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to define lasting remission, allowed treatment, relevant exposures and protective-response tests, then track relapse, retreatment and harms after dosing. This would distinguish sustained benefit from temporary improvement.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce treatment and identify responders
milestones.explanation: Independent trials would have to reproduce benefits, identify responding patients and targets, and establish a consistent medicine, dose and schedule. This would define reliable treatment and its practical boundaries.

milestones.label: Restoration, memory erasure and added protection receive distinct proof
milestones.explanation: Separate studies would have to safely restore responses, distinguish memory erasure from continued restraint, and establish useful protection with added control beyond vaccination. Successful tolerance alone would not establish these abilities.

uncertain: How long must remission last, and under what exposures and background treatment, to count as durable?
How broadly must unrelated immune responses be tested to establish retained protection?
What additional control would establishing a protective response offer beyond existing vaccination?

page.title: Pharmacological induction of antigen-specific immune tolerance
page.definition: An administered medicine establishes disease control that persists after treatment ends by selectively quieting responses to a chosen antigen, a molecular target recognised by the immune system, while preserving protective responses to unrelated antigens.

goal.need: Coeliac disease affects more than 1% of the global population. In the 146-child IMPACT trial, peanut-allergy remission occurred in a minority after 134 weeks of oral immunotherapy and 26 weeks without treatment or peanut. NIAID defines the therapeutic goal as selective elimination of pathogenic responses with protective immunity preserved and no continued tolerance-inducing treatment.

figures.caption: Peanut-allergy remission after treatment withdrawal in IMPACT, published in 2022
figures.note: Participants were aged 12 to younger than 48 months. Remission required passing a double-blind, placebo-controlled challenge with 5000 mg peanut protein.

statements.quote: Antigen-specific tolerance induction is a major goal for the treatment or prevention of autoimmune disease and graft rejection
Immune tolerance-inducing therapies reprogramme immune cells to eliminate pathogenic immune responses while preserving protective immunity.

completion.title: An antigen-directed medicine induces off-treatment tolerance while preserving protective immunity.
completion.criterion: Following an administered antigen-directed treatment, humans show selective elimination of pathogenic immune responses to the relevant antigens while preserving protective immunity, without ongoing treatment with the tolerance-inducing intervention. NIAID's definition specifies no minimum follow-up duration, responder fraction or protective-antigen panel. The clinical and immunological components must coexist; a target biomarker change or remission over one withdrawal interval alone does not establish the combined phenotype.
completion.set_by: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, RFA-AI-12-043, Section I, 'Purpose' (2012 definition of immune tolerance).
completion.threshold_quote: while preserving protective immunity and does not require ongoing treatment with the intervention.
completion.basis: This published programme definition contains the three components of the capability: antigen selectivity, protective immunity and persistence without continued intervention. It provides a functional criterion rather than a numerical validation protocol. IMPACT establishes remission through a defined withdrawal interval; TAK-101 establishes a target-specific immune effect. Neither result alone establishes the complete phenotype.

milestones.title: An antigen-directed treatment reduces an animal's response to its target in a controlled challenge.
milestones.criterion: After antigen-directed treatment, an antigen challenge elicits a lower target-specific antibody or T-cell response than control treatment. This is the experimental oral-tolerance convention; the textbook gives no fixed effect-size cutoff. In 2020, TIMP-GLIA gliadin nanoparticles reduced gliadin responses in mouse models; delayed-hypersensitivity experiments used five mice per group. These experiments do not establish human remission.
milestones.set_by: Experimental oral-tolerance convention described in Janeway's Immunobiology, tenth edition; the textbook's worked example uses ovalbumin in mice.
milestones.threshold_quote: Mice that were fed ovalbumin have a lower ovalbumin-specific systemic immune response than that of mice fed the control protein.

milestones.title: An antigen-directed investigational medicine is administered to people in a phase 1 study.
milestones.criterion: An antigen-directed medicine reaches initial human administration in a phase 1 study evaluating its pharmacology and adverse effects. ACeD enrolled 41 adults with coeliac disease between 7 February 2020 and 8 October 2021; KAN-101 caused no dose-limiting toxicities. A 2017 proinsulin-peptide study analysed 27 adults with new-onset type 1 diabetes and reported no systemic or local hypersensitivity. These results establish human exposure and observed tolerability.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Drug Development and Review Definitions, 'Phase I Clinical Studies'.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: An antigen-directed medicine reduces its target response in a controlled human antigen-challenge study.
milestones.criterion: Meet a prespecified target-antigen immune-response endpoint against a control group. The TAK-101 coeliac protocol measured gliadin-specific interferon-γ-producing blood cells on challenge day 6. The 2021 report's immune analysis included 13 TAK-101 and 16 placebo recipients: mean increases were 2.01 versus 17.58 spot-forming units per million cells (P=0.006). Anti-CD3 responses were similar; this polyclonal stimulation does not test unrelated vaccine protection. The histology comparison, involving 13 TAK-101 and 15 placebo recipients, was not significant (P=0.08).
milestones.set_by: TAK-101 Study Group, registered phase 2a study NCT03738475; assay and challenge particulars were published for coeliac disease.
milestones.threshold_quote: change from baseline in T-cell–mediated, gluten-stimulated IFN-γ production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) on day 6 of gluten challenge

milestones.title: An antigen-directed medicine produces clinical remission after treatment withdrawal.
milestones.criterion: Meet a prespecified off-treatment clinical-remission endpoint under the disease's protocol. IMPACT defined peanut remission as passing a double-blind, placebo-controlled challenge with a cumulative 5000 mg peanut protein 26 weeks after discontinuation, following 134 weeks of treatment. Its published results establish remission in some children, not permanent tolerance or preserved unrelated protective immunity. This numerical test does not define remission in coeliac disease or type 1 diabetes.
milestones.set_by: Immune Tolerance Network, IMPACT study NCT03345160; its numerical remission endpoint is specific to peanut allergy.
milestones.threshold_quote: remission, defined as passing the 5000 mg DBPCFC 26 weeks after oral immunotherapy discontinuation;

not_found: No common numerical definition of off-treatment remission across these three diseases was found.
No universal duration or protective-immunity assay threshold for antigen-specific immune tolerance was found.
The ClinicalTrials.gov results pages for KAN-101 studies NCT05574010 and NCT06001177 returned no readable study data.
The full KAN-101 journal article could not be opened.
No published completion criteria for deliberately reversing tolerance or selectively erasing antigen-specific immune memory were found.

results.finding: In phase 1, 21 adults received KAN-101 in part B; 16 reported treatment-related adverse events.
results.detail: The study also assessed pharmacokinetics. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred.
results.quote: Treatment-related adverse events were reported in 11 (79%) of 14 patients in part A and 18 (67%) of 27 in part B (placebo two [33%] of six patients; KAN-101 16 [76%] of 21 patients), were grade 2 or lower, and were mild to moderate in severity.

results.finding: In the per-protocol sample of 93 children, peanut immunotherapy reduced peanut-specific IgE versus placebo.
results.detail: Immune markers were measured longitudinally and compared between groups. The paper does not establish that a prespecified immune-response endpoint elicited by the peanut challenge was met.
results.quote: Compared with placebo, peanut oral immunotherapy decreased peanut-specific and Ara h2-specific IgE, skin prick test, and basophil activation, and increased peanut-specific and Ara h2-specific IgG4 at weeks 134 and 160.

results.finding: Peanut immunotherapy induced remission in 20 of 96 children, versus 1 of 50 receiving placebo.
results.detail: Remission was the prespecified key secondary outcome: passing a 5000 mg peanut challenge 26 weeks after treatment ended. Missing challenges were counted as failures.
results.quote: After avoidance, 20 (21%, 95% CI 13–30) of 96 participants receiving peanut oral immunotherapy compared with one (2%, 0·05–11) of 50 receiving placebo met remission criteria (RD 19%, 95% CI 10–28; p=0·0021).

results.finding: In a phase 1b study, 27 adults were randomized; 19 received proinsulin peptide.
results.detail: The study assessed safety and immune effects. No hypersensitivity reactions were observed during treatment.

results.finding: 18 children completed a challenge; the treatment group ingested a median 1710 mg of peanut protein.
results.detail: The challenge followed 12 months of dosing; the study did not examine outcomes after stopping therapy.
results.quote: During the double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge, the treatment group safely ingested 20 times more peanut protein than the placebo group (median 1710 mg vs. 85 mg, p=0.011).

results.finding: In a phase IIb trial, 109 people received an injection; adverse events occurred in 49% of the active-treatment group.
results.detail: The study establishes human exposure and reports tolerability, but it was a phase IIb trial, not an initial phase 1 study.

results.finding: In a trial of 109 people, GAD-alum recipients had increased GAD antibodies versus placebo; the immune-analysis sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The study measured target-specific immune responses, including responses of blood cells stimulated with GAD65 outside the body. It did not report a prespecified target-response endpoint met in a human antigen-challenge study.

results.finding: BHT-3021 in 80 adults with type 1 diabetes: no serious adverse events related to the medicine were reported.
results.detail: The study evaluated safety and immune responses after administration, but the supplied text does not identify it as a phase 1 study.
results.quote: No serious adverse events related to BHT-3021 occurred.

results.finding: In 23 adults with type 1 diabetes receiving injected insulin, median insulin antibody concentrations were 4.7 versus 17 units/mL after nasal insulin versus placebo.
results.detail: The insulin antibody response to injected insulin was a primary endpoint. Injected insulin was started when clinically indicated, so participants began it at different times and only a subset received it. Nasal insulin did not slow the loss of β-cell function.
results.quote:
By 24 months, IA concentration in participants receiving subcutaneous insulin was significantly lower in the 12 who had received nasal insulin (4.7 [2.3–11] units/mL) than in the 11 who had received nasal placebo (17 [6.0–32] units/mL) (
P
= 0.019)
